newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rally, Dow sets first record in three weeks.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally, Dow sets first record in three weeks.

text.p: Stocks rallied for the second straight session Monday, pushing the Dow Jones industrial average to its 14th record of the year.
Companies with strong brand names and oil producers led the way, and the market got a boost from news of the latest surge of cash into mutual funds, investors and analysts said.
"It looks like the big boys are back buying the big stocks," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
The 30-share Dow jumped 78.50 points to 7,079.39 after adding 56 points on Friday on a government report of solid job growth in February with little sign of wage-driven inflation.
The Dow close eclipsed the previous record of 7,067.46 set on Feb. 18 though most other major market gauges remained well off record levels. The Dow set 44 records for all of 1996.
In the broader market, winners beat losers, 1,639 to 856, on moderate New York Stock Exchange volume of 458.7 million shares.
Bargain-hunting helped high-technology stocks shake off their recent woes, though most of Monday's gains were confined to bigger blue-chip issues.

News of a fresh surge of cash into mutual funds also helped stocks, analysts said. Americans put $1.49 billion into mutual funds for the three days ended on Thursday, compared with $7 million for the two days ended on March 3, according to Mutual Fund Trim Tab, which tracks the industry.
The figures often vary widely.
As in the past, fund managers seemed to be pouring the new cash directly into big stocks, analysts said.
But in a departure from recent sessions, investors seemed to be sifting through the technology sector, looking for bargains created by the group's recent sell-off.

"People are nibbling away at some of these stocks," said Arnie Owen, director of equity trading at Kaufman Brothers, noting some technology issues have fallen 40 percent in recent weeks. "When you get a situation like that, that's when you start to see bargain hunting," he said.

The Nasdaq composite index, heavily weighted with technology stocks, rose 10.92 points to 1,322.72, a smaller percentage gain than that posted by the Dow and one that kept it well below its record of 1,388.06 set on Jan. 22.
With technology issues lagging and interest still focused on big blue chips, analysts were reluctant to predict the market was poised for a new surge.
"I don't think we're at the rally stage yet," said Barbara Marcin, vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management. "This looks like it could be a little bit of index chasing."
Consumer-oriented issues were the Dow's strongest components, with Procter & Gamble Co. rising 4-1/4 to 124-3/4 and Philip Morris Cos. adding 2-3/4 to 138-3/4.
Oil shares also fuelled the rally. Texaco added 2 to 105, Exxon gained 2-5/8 to 103 and Chevron was up 1-1/4 to 67-3/8.
Among technology stocks, Cisco Systems gained 2 to 53-3/8, shrugging off news that PaineWebber had downgraded the maker of network computer equipment to neutral from buy.
U.S. Robotics rose 2-3/8 to 58-3/4 after the maker of computer modems said it was introducing a system to provide Internet access over cable television.
Microsoft added 3-1/4 to 100 and International Business Machines rose 1-3/8 to 146-1/8.
Office Depot tumbled 5-1/2 to 17-1/8 after the Federal Trade Commission said it would seek to block the company's planned merger with Staples Inc. Staples lost 1-5/16 to 23-1/4.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 8.68 points to 813.65. The American Stock Exchange index added 1.57 to 603.63.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks rose 3.87 to a record 427.70, edging past the old mark of 427.07 set on Feb. 18. The average share rose 40 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,757.044, up 69.926, or 0.91 percent.
